result.reason: The passage is the mishna about hekdesh goring cases (shor re'ehu exclusion), which exactly matches the 'Mishna: Hekdesh Cases' section prose describing this very mishna and its exemption in both directions.

The passage is the mishna text about an ox of a Jew goring a gentile's ox (exempt) versus a gentile's ox goring a Jew's ox (full damages, whether tam or mu'ad), which is exactly what the 'Non-Jew Cases in Mishna' section's prose describes and analyzes.

All four items cover exactly the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, the logical problem of re'ehu davka vs. lav davka, the kal vachomer proposal, and the dayo objection — all of which are explicitly discussed in candidate 0's prose, before Reish Lakish's resolution which belongs to candidate 1.

Both items present Reish Lakish's argument that the default is full damages and that re'ehu by tam excludes hekdesh from the half-damages reduction, which is precisely what the 'Reish Lakish Solution' prose describes.

The passage presents the exact 'whichever way you look at it' (mimah nafshach) dilemma regarding re'ehu and the gentile's ox, which is precisely what Rav Yosef's Logic prose describes as the structural difficulty that leads Rav Yosef to abandon re'ehu and turn to the Habakkuk verse instead.

The passage is Rabbi Abbahu's statement deriving from Habakkuk 3:6 that God permitted the nations' money to Israel because they did not fulfill the seven Noahide commandments — this is precisely the content discussed in Rav Yosef's Logic section, which explicitly analyzes this same Habakkuk verse and its interpretation.

The passage quotes Rabbi Yoḥanan deriving the damage law from 'v'hofia me-Har Paran,' which is explicitly discussed in candidate 3's prose as one of the two pesukim cited in the beraita alongside Rav Yosef's verse, with the Gemara explaining why two verses are needed.

Both items are the baraita stating the exemption/liability rule for ox-goring cases involving Jews and gentiles, followed by the Gemara's question about why a second verse is needed — precisely what the prose under 'Tanya on Non-Jew Cases' describes.

All four items directly present the Rav Mattana and Rav Yosef expositions of 'amad vayimoded eretz,' including the gezerah shavah for exile and the objection/resolution about the sinner being rewarded — exactly the content described in the 'Rav Matna & Rav Yosef' prose.

The passage opens with 'But do they not receive reward?' — it is the Gemara's challenge introducing the reward question, which belongs under 'Reward for Non-Jews' whose prose explicitly frames this as the deeper question raised and notes that Rabbi Meir's statement provides the answer, making it the natural home for this transitional challenge-plus-answer unit.

The passage directly quotes the Gemara's resolution using Rabbi Chanina's principle about metzuveh v'oseh vs. eino metzuveh v'oseh, which is exactly what the 'Aino Metzuveh Resolution' prose discusses in detail.

Both items together constitute the complete Roman officers story (the arrival/study/departure critique plus the mimah nafshach argument and decision not to report), which belongs under heading 0 'Roman Officers & Torah' whose prose describes exactly this narrative arc — the officers studying Torah three times and the full episode — rather than being split across the 'Officers' Critique' and 'Officers' Discretion' headings.

The passage describes exactly what the prose under 'Ulla's Theology' discusses: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's daughter dying, the rabbis asking Ulla to accompany them for consolation, and Ulla's refusal on the grounds that Babylonian condolences constitute blasphemy.

All three items together form the complete kal vachomer story — Moses's reasoning, the Moabite inference, and God's response about Ruth and Naamah — which is exactly what heading 0's prose describes in full, including the shtei preidot conclusion.
The passage is the exact kal vachomer argument about two virtuous fledglings and God's compassion over two nations that Candidate 0's prose explicitly analyzes and quotes in detail.

The passage directly states that God does not deprive any creature of its reward, even for pleasant speech — which is exactly what the 'God's Reward System' section discusses, while the 'Daughters' Merit' section discusses the specific illustration from Lot's daughters that follows as a consequence of this principle.

Both items discuss the contrast between Moab and Ammon regarding forced labor/angarya, which is precisely what the 'Daughters' Merit' prose describes in detail, including the modesty/tzniut angle and the differential treatment of the two daughters' descendants.
